question.name: CSEC Phy Jan 2023 Q6b — Define Isotopes
question.text:
Define the term 'isotopes' by completing the statement below:

Isotopes are atoms of the same [[1]] that have the same number of [[2]] but different numbers of [[3]] in their nuclei.
question.general_feedback:
Definition of isotopes:

Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons (same atomic number Z) but different numbers of neutrons (different mass numbers A).

Example: Carbon-12 (⁶¹²C) and Carbon-14 (⁶¹⁴C) are isotopes — both have 6 protons (Z=6) but C-12 has 6 neutrons and C-14 has 8 neutrons.

Key point: Since the number of protons defines the element, isotopes are always the same element. Isotopes may differ in radioactivity (e.g. C-14 is radioactive; C-12 is stable).

ddwtos.cloze_html: Isotopes are atoms of the same [[1]] that have the same number of [[2]] but different numbers of [[3]] in their nuclei.

groups.label: Isotopes are atoms of the same ___
groups.diagnostic_hint: Isotopes are atoms of the same ELEMENT — they have the same number of protons (same atomic number), which defines the element. For example, all carbon isotopes have 6 protons.

groups.label: Isotopes have the same number of ___
groups.diagnostic_hint: Isotopes have the same number of PROTONS (= atomic number). This is what makes them the same element. For carbon: always 6 protons, whether C-12, C-13, or C-14.

groups.label: Isotopes differ in the number of ___
groups.diagnostic_hint: Isotopes differ in the number of NEUTRONS. Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons, Carbon-13 has 7, Carbon-14 has 8 — all are carbon because they have 6 protons. Different neutron counts give different mass numbers.

ddwtos.word_bank_note: 8 tokens for 3 slots. Group 1 (element): 'mass number' is a critical distractor — students sometimes confuse isotopes (same Z, different A) and confusingly write 'same mass number' which is the opposite. 'atom' and 'nucleus' are too vague. Group 2 (same number of protons): 'electrons' — the number of electrons also equals protons in a neutral atom, so electrons is technically true, but CSEC mark schemes require 'protons' as the defining nuclear property. Group 3 (different neutrons): 'protons' is wrong (swapping protons and neutrons is the most common error in this question). 'nucleons' is wrong — isotopes can differ in nucleon count (A) since A = p + n and n differs.
